label: Variational Principles
notes: Welcome to Lecture 19, spanning printed pages 111 through 118. We replace force laws with a single scalar functional and ask which path makes it stationary. The whole lecture is one arc: from action, to the Euler-Lagrange equations, to the convexity hypotheses that turn a critical path into an honest minimizer.

label: From Newton to Action
notes: Start with a conservative force, the negative gradient of a potential. Newton's equation is recovered, but reformulated: instead of integrating a force in time, nature selects the path that makes the time integral of kinetic minus potential energy stationary. Emphasize that this is a statement about whole curves, not pointwise dynamics.

label: The Lagrangian on TM
notes: The natural home of the Lagrangian is the tangent bundle. A point and a velocity together, the lift of the curve, are the arguments of L. Make clear that L lives on TM while the conjugate momentum and Hamiltonian will later live on the cotangent bundle; the Legendre transform is the bridge between them.

label: The Action Functional
notes: Define the action as the time integral of the Lagrangian along the lifted curve. Stress that the action is a function whose domain is an infinite-dimensional space of paths with fixed endpoints. Minimizing or making it stationary is a calculus problem on that path space, which motivates the variation we set up next.

label: Endpoint-Fixed Variation
notes: Introduce a one-parameter family of paths sharing the same endpoints, so the variation field vanishes at both ends. Differentiate the action in the family parameter at zero. The picture shows perturbed paths fanning around the true trajectory; the action graph is flat at the center, which is exactly the stationarity we want to characterize.

label: Euler-Lagrange Equations
notes: Differentiate under the integral, then integrate by parts to move the time derivative off the variation field. The boundary term dies because endpoints are fixed. Since the variation is otherwise arbitrary, the bracket must vanish, giving the Euler-Lagrange equation. This is the precise critical-point condition for the action functional.

label: The Legendre Condition
notes: Walk through the ledger of three cases from the notebook. With no velocity dependence the equation is a pointwise critical-set condition; affine velocity dependence gives a singular velocity Hessian and only first-order content; a nondegenerate velocity Hessian is what makes Euler-Lagrange a genuine second-order law solvable from initial position and velocity.

label: Stationary Is Not Minimal
notes: A solution of Euler-Lagrange is only a critical point. The second variation decides whether it is a local minimum. Show the harmonic-oscillator window formula: the second variation is positive precisely when the interval is shorter than pi over omega. Beyond that length the critical path becomes a saddle, so length of the interval genuinely matters.

label: Tonelli: Minimizers Exist
notes: State the Tonelli philosophy: strict convexity of L in the velocity variable plus suitable growth gives lower semicontinuity and coercivity, so a minimizer exists in the path space. Convexity in velocity is the same hypothesis seen two ways, locally as a positive velocity Hessian and globally as existence of minimizers.

label: TM to T*M
notes: Connect the variational and Hamiltonian pictures. The fiber derivative of L sends a velocity to a momentum, mapping TM to the cotangent bundle. When the Legendre condition holds this is a local diffeomorphism, and the Hamiltonian is the Legendre transform of L. Euler-Lagrange on TM becomes Hamilton's equations on T-star-M.

label: Geodesics and Recap
notes: Close with the kinetic Lagrangian, one half the metric norm squared. Its Euler-Lagrange equation is the geodesic equation, and constant-speed geodesics minimize both action and length on short arcs, as the sphere comparison confirms. Recap the arc: action, Euler-Lagrange, Legendre, convexity, and the bridge to Hamiltonian dynamics.
